#634. Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike

Germany's biggest single union, IG Metall, is calling on car and shipyard workers to strike amid a pay row. Meanwhile, Germany's president is setting off on an Africa trip. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:

Bosses at soccer team Bayern Munich have publicly questioned whether young Germany international Jamal Musiala's contract is valid in view of a debilitating neurological condition.

The remarks have been criticized by media and from several other quarters, among them the global players' union FIFPRO, which accused the officials of neglecting their "duty of care" toward their players.

You can read details on what has been happening at the top football club in this DW article: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

Friedrich Christian "Mick" Flick, an art collector, investor and multimillionaire who belonged to one of Germany's richest business dynasties, has died aged 82 in Rosenheim in the southern state of Bavaria, his family has said.

The family said in a statement issued on Saturday that Flick left behind "the memory of a life shaped by significant acts of generosity as a donor and patron, particularly in contemporary art and in promoting tolerance."

Flick was the grandson of Friedrich Flick, who made a huge fortune in the Nazi era with his coal and steel business, partly by using forced labor.

This past came back to haunt the grandson in 2003 when he pledged to loan his world-famous collection of modern art to Berlin, with the Central Council of Jews in Germany calling the Flick Collection a "Göring Collection" and saying the loan was intended to wash clean the "blood money" from the Nazi era.

The collection, which contains some 2,500 works by 150 artists, was exhibited in parts in the German capital from 2004 to 2021.

Flick later said in an interview that the widespread outrage, while hurtful, had forced him to look more closely at his family's history.

According to his family, Flick once said: "I have no guilt for my forefathers' conduct, but I feel a responsibility, a very special responsibility. Every German bears this responsibility. As a Flick, I bear it twice."

Among other things, he collaborated with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees Berlin's museums, to research his family's Nazi past.

He also set up a foundation in Potsdam, near Berlin, that aimed to combat xenophobia and racism and contributed €5 million ($5.4 million) to the foundation to compensate former forced laborers.

The family was also involved in a highly publicized party donations scandal in the 1980s that became known as the "Flick Affair."

"Mick" Flick married Countess Maya von Schönburg (1958-2019), the older sister of well-known socialite, businesswoman, art collector and artist Gloria von Thurn und Taxis, in 1985. The couple had three children.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.

On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.

The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.

In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.

The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has said it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.

It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an important bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.

The BfG said it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.

The rising water level in the Rhine, an important shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.

"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," said Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.

In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.

He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.

The conservation NGO also said that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.

It said species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), said she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She said that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages."

The proposals are currently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

The powerful IG Metall union said on Sunday it would call another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues.

Altogether, some 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany have been called upon to participate, including employees at automaker Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilding company Meyer Werft and wind ​energy company Siemens Gamesa.

The union said that a strike on Friday saw some 12,300 workers walk out at 17 facilities.

It says that the strikes are meant to increase the pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% ‌wage increase.

So far, employers have ⁠offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.

A new goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.

After scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.

Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.

However, he did not perform the controversial part of his usual goal celebration. In it, he removes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling.

This celebration has been heavily criticized, even by Dortmund's fan department.

Nmecha explained that the celebrations is about "putting down my 'crown' in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength."

The gesture is used by Ballers in God, a network of Christian football players that has been criticized for the homophobic and queerphobic statements made by its members.

Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke said he asked the player not to do the celebration again.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday.

Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.

Fourth-place RB Leipzig had five different players score in a 5-1 victory over Union Berlin, bringing them to 21 points. Bayer Leverkusen scored four unanswered goals against Paderborn to stay in fifth place.

Germany is seeking to redress years of underinvestment by pouring billions into the modernization of public infrastructure and digital networks, and the transition to renewable energy sources.

Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.

According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.

Operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.

Bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.

"We have achieved another record year," CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said. "This shows that our club has a strong foundation. And we continue to invest to ensure the best possible conditions for the sporting success of our teams."

Moreover, Bayern achieved another milestone. They reached 500,000 members — more than any other club in the world.

Over the past 12 years, the German giants have doubled their membership, growing from 250,000 in 2014 to 500,000 this year.

"Record champions, record members, record member champions," president Herbert Hainer said.

Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.

The remaining 30% is owned by four German companies with roots in Bavaria: Adidas, Audi, Allianz, and Viessmann.

Bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.

England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.

#633. Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

New observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole. An international research team led by MPE has traced these compact clouds to a massive pair of stars whose powerful winds appear to produce material that could eventually help feed the black hole, known as Sagittarius A*.

The center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment. At its core sits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a supermassive black hole surrounded by stars, gas, and dust moving through a region dominated by intense gravitational forces. This extreme setting gives astronomers an opportunity to investigate how matter moves near black holes and where the material that sustains their activity comes from.

Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*. These mysterious "clumps" may provide important clues about how material makes its way toward the black hole. However, scientists have struggled to determine where the clouds originate and what causes them to form.

Mysterious Gas Clouds Near the Milky Way's Black Hole

One of the first major discoveries came in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of ionized gas called G2. Containing several times Earth's mass, the cloud produces emissions from hydrogen and helium, consistent with hot gas mixed with dust. It follows a highly elongated orbit around Sagittarius A* and has a faint extension trailing behind it, known as G2t.

Soon afterward, researchers examining older observations recognized another similar object, G1, traveling along a closely related path. The similarities suggested that G1, G2, and G2t might not be independent objects. Instead, they could represent concentrations of gas within a larger, continuous stream.

Even relatively small differences in gas density can make such a stream appear broken into separate clouds. This happens because the brightness of the gas increases in proportion to the square of its density, making denser regions stand out much more strongly.

More recently, astronomers observed gas in G2's trailing material gathering into another compact cloud that follows a similar orbit. Although this newly formed object might naturally be called G3, that designation had already been assigned to a different object. Together, the related clouds trace a connected flow of material through the Galactic Center, known as the G1-2-3 streamer.

These clouds could play a surprisingly important role in sustaining the black hole. Calculations suggest that if approximately one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, it could provide enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity. Discovering how the clouds form could therefore help explain how the black hole receives its supply of matter.

Astronomers Trace the Gas Clouds to Their Source

Researchers have considered several possible explanations for the clouds, including powerful winds from massive stars, stellar explosions such as novae, and gas pulled away from objects by the black hole's gravity.

To investigate, the MPE-led team used two advanced infrared spectrographs, SINFONI and ERIS. Both instruments employ adaptive optics to produce sharper observations. By examining a specific hydrogen emission feature called the Brackett‑γ line, the astronomers measured the clouds' positions and velocities and reconstructed their paths around Sagittarius A*.

The results revealed a striking pattern. G1, G2, and G2t all follow orbits with nearly the same shape and orientation. It would be extraordinarily unlikely for three unrelated clouds to share such closely matching orbital characteristics, strongly suggesting that they originated from the same source.

Two Massive Stars May Be Creating the Clouds

By working backward from the clouds' observed motions and their velocities along our line of sight, the researchers identified a promising source: IRS 16SW, a massive contact binary system consisting of two stars in extremely close proximity.

The stellar pair belongs to a disk of young stars that revolves clockwise around Sagittarius A*. Its location and motion provide a plausible explanation for the gas stream. Even the slight differences between the clouds' orbital paths can be accounted for by the movement of the two stars around one another.

Computer simulations of how gas flows and interacts provided additional support for this explanation. The models indicate that powerful stellar winds from the binary system can collide with surrounding material, creating a shock in the region between the stars. Gas then accumulates and becomes compressed, forming dense concentrations that can eventually separate from the system.

Once released, these compact clouds can travel inward along paths resembling those observed in the G1-2-3 streamer. This provides a physical explanation for how one binary star system could produce several distinct clouds moving along closely related orbits.

A New Clue to How Supermassive Black Holes Are Fed

The findings suggest that massive stars near the Galactic Center may provide a continuing supply of gas capable of fueling Sagittarius A*. Rather than relying only on material already circulating around the black hole, the system could receive fresh gas from the powerful winds generated by nearby stars.

The discovery also brings together several important processes in astronomy. The evolution of massive stars, the movement and compression of gas, and the supply of material to supermassive black holes may all be closely connected. By identifying a possible source of the mysterious clouds near Sagittarius A*, researchers have uncovered a new way in which stars could help sustain black hole activity at the heart of our own galaxy.

#632. Olivia Rodrigo Shares Second Holiday Song ‘Miss This Christmas’ on Amazon Music

The new track follows the pop star's debut holiday song, "Take Me Home (4 Christmas)."

Olivia Rodrigo is keeping the holiday spirit alive with another festive release.

Just weeks after making her Christmas debut with “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” the 23-year-old pop star has returned with a second holiday offering, “Miss This Christmas,” exclusively through Amazon Music.

Rodrigo debuted “Miss This Christmas” live during her concert at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Monday (Nov. 23), introducing it to the crowd as a “really sad Christmas song” and noting that “no one’s ever really heard it before,” according to Rolling Stone.

The track was also included as the B-side on the vinyl edition of “Take Me Home (4 Christmas),” which arrived in early November. The holiday tune peaked at No. 32 on the Billboard Hot 100 in mid-November.

While “Take Me Home (4 Christmas)” leans into festive pop with a nostalgic feel, “Miss This Christmas” takes a more melancholy approach, exploring the heartache of missing someone during the holiday season.

“Happy Christmas to the lonely/ Broken hearts that feel just like me,” Rodrigo sings before adding, “Yeah, next year’s gonna look real different/ Tell your folks I’ll miss their Christmas.”

The new release arrives during a particularly busy stretch for Rodrigo, who earned seven nominations at the 2027 Grammy Awards, including album of the year for her third studio album, you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love.

“I am over the moon!!!!!” Rodrigo wrote on Instagram after the Grammy noms were announced. “I love this album so much and for it to be recognized in this way is the biggest honor.”

You seem pretty sad for a girl so in love also recently earned its fifth nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

#631. 'Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home' at 40: 'Trek' has never been as joyous or fun as in 'the one with the whales'

Colorful metaphors, a near-miss with Eddie Murphy and humpback whales in 20th-century California.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales".

After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp?

Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.

They gave him freedom to tell the story he wanted to tell, and he landed on a not obviously box-office-friendly formula of "No dying, no fighting, no shooting, no photon torpedoes, no phaser blasts, no stereotypical bad guy". It was a massive shift away from Khan and Kruge, the grandstanding villains in movies II and III.

Nimoy also wanted the film to have an environmental message and appeal beyond the franchise's traditional fanbase. The film would actually be promoted with minimal "Trek" branding in some territories.

"I wanted to make it accessible to people who don't go to 'Star Trek' movies," Nimoy said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman. "I wanted to make it a movie-movie. It starts out like a 'Star Trek' movie and then makes a left turn. It is intentionally very different."

"The Voyage Home" effectively closes the trilogy that began four years earlier with "The Wrath of Khan". The story picks up three months after Spock's regenerated body is reunited with his katra (spirit), though nobody ever explains why Kirk and the rest of the crew are all still wearing exactly the same clothes. Following the self-destruction of Enterprise over the Genesis Planet, the gang are heading back to Earth to face the music for a lengthy rap sheet that includes grand theft starship and insubordination on an epic scale.

But as they voyage home (geddit?) in a reconditioned Klingon Bird-of-Prey nicknamed the Bounty — complete with a cloaking device that will come in very handy when hiding in Golden Gate Park — they learn that an alien probe of unknown origin (one of the coolest "Star Trek" spaceships) is tearing Earth apart looking for humpback whales. With the species extinct since the 21st century, the crew travel back in time via one of the most surreal sequences in "Star Trek" history — Morphing CG heads? What the hell was Nimoy thinking? — in the hope of finding the whales that might just be able to ask politely if the probe might leave us alone.

Screenwriters Steve Meerson and Peter Krikes were assigned to the project early on (working with Nimoy and producer Harve Bennett on the story), and their treatments included a future Earth under threat from a plague and a discarded subplot about Lt. Saavik being pregnant with Spock's child as a result of the pon farr mating ritual. There were also discussions about the Bird-of-Prey decloaking above the Super Bowl, and — most bizarrely of all — a guest-starring role for Eddie Murphy as an astrophysicist who wants to believe in aliens.

Murphy was both a Trekkie and one of the biggest stars on the planet at the time but ultimately decided to make notorious stinker "The Golden Child" instead. "In retrospect, I think I might have been better off doing 'Star Trek IV'," he said later. Paramount had also gotten cold feet about putting the star of the highly lucrative "Beverly Hills Cop" in its highest-profile franchise.

"Paramount said, 'We're not going to put out [our] two most valuable assets in one movie – so start over, folks!'" said Nicholas Meyer (h/t The Telegraph), hired to retool the script after Murphy's departure. "That's why I was called at the last minute."

Meyer was already "Star Trek" royalty, having brought the movie series to life as director and uncredited writer of "The Wrath of Khan". Indeed, he's arguably the reason the "odd numbers bad/even numbers good" theory of "Trek" films persisted for so long, having later gone on to co-write and direct "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country".

He shared scripting duties with Bennett, with the producer writing the 23rd-century-set bookends of the film, and Meyer handling everything in present-day California. Weirdly, Meyer had prior experience bringing a time traveler to contemporary San Francisco in his 1979 HG Wells/Jack the Ripper adventure "Time After Time".

With the three previous "Star Trek" movies largely studio-based, "The Voyage Home" marked a rare chance for cast and crew to head out on location. The Monterey Bay Aquarium filled in for the Cetacean Institute (slightly implausible home of humpbacks George and Gracie), while the USS Ranger — moored in San Diego and no stranger to Hollywood after "Top Gun" — guest-starred as a nuclear "wessel".

Kirk and co. also headed out onto the streets of San Francisco. Nimoy had toyed with giving them '80s-appropriate disguises, but changed his mind when he realized nobody would bat an eyelid at their 23rd-century civilian attire.

Aside from some second unit work photographing humpbacks off the coast of Hawaii, the whales themselves were mostly animatronics created by Industrial Light & Magic. "One of the reasons we think that ['The Voyage Home'] really didn't win visual-effects awards is people didn't really understand how good [the whales were]," said executive producer Ralph Winter. "ILM did such a good job on those whales that they went on tour for a year or more around the world to museums because the expertise, the art, and science of what they had done was very good."

Meyer, meanwhile, fully embraced the opportunity to write a fish-out-of-water comedy, with this seasoned crew of Starfleet veterans struggling to get their heads around the eccentricities of late 20th-century America.

Kirk and Spock experiment extensively with "colorful metaphors" — "double dumbass on you!" — while Kirk gets out of paying for dinner by using the convenient excuse that money isn't a thing in the future. Scotty (James Doohan) attempts to talk to a mid-'80s Apple Macintosh via a mouse before he risks screwing with the timeline by 'inventing' transparent aluminum decades early.

And in the film's most famous moment, Spock delivers a Vulcan neck pinch to a punk playing his music very loudly on a public bus, winning extensive applause from his fellow passengers in the process. The nuisance rocker was played by Nimoy's assistant, Kirk Thatcher, who co-wrote the "I Hate You" song that plays on that era-authentic ghetto blaster. He later returned to the role in "Star Trek: Picard", though this time he responded more apologetically to Seven of Nine's request to turn it down.

Kirk is undoubtedly the center of the movie, pulling the strings and getting his first romantic interest since the Original Series — whale expert Dr Gillian Taylor (Catherine Hicks), who eventually accompanies the Enterprisers back to the future. But "The Voyage Home" also gives the supporting bridge crew — all of whom reveal a talent for comedy — more satisfying character beats than they'd ever had before. Walter Koenig's W-heavy pronunciation of "vessels" would later be adopted by Anton Yelchin when he inherited the role in JJ Abrams' "Star Trek".

The crew eventually makes it out of the 20th century alive, with the whales safely secured in a giant fish tank so they can make contact with the probe. Of course, what George and Gracie actually say when they arrive in the future remains a mystery; despite Bennett's insistence that the whale song conversation should be subtitled, he was wisely overruled by Nimoy.

With Earth saved from death by giant cigar, the Enterprise crew have all their charges revoked, bar one, as Kirk is 'busted' down to Captain. The crew is then gifted the shiny new USS Enterprise-A, freeing them to continue exploring the cosmos on the big screen.

Which they did, with Shatner taking advantage of a so-called "favored nations" clause in his contract — which meant Paramount had to match anything offered to Nimoy — to direct the rather less positively received "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier", before Meyer returned for "The Undiscovered Country".

Nimoy delivered on his promise to appeal beyond the traditional fanbase, and his reward for earning "Star Trek"'s biggest ever box office haul — a record "The Voyage Home" would hold until Abrams went Trekkin' in 2009 — was directing smash-hit comedy "Three Men and a Baby" the following year. The film also paved the way for "The Next Generation", as Paramount realized the franchise's massive potential, but decided they wanted to cash in without paying mega-bucks for the legacy cast.

Hardcore fans will often claim they prefer the more serious themes of "The Wrath of Khan", "First Contact" or even "The Motion Picture" to "The Voyage Home", but "Star Trek" has rarely been as joyous or fun as on this madcap jaunt to the 20th century. "The One with the Whales" really is one for the ages.

'Star Trek: The Voyage Home' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

#629. Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed

Reaching another star will require spacecraft capable of traveling far faster than anything humanity has built so far. Conventional rockets powered by chemical fuel simply cannot achieve the enormous speeds needed to cross the distances between stars within a practical amount of time. One promising alternative is the solar sail, a vast, lightweight reflective surface that uses the momentum of light to propel a spacecraft through space.

Some proposed interstellar missions would take this concept even further by using powerful lasers to push sails to extraordinary speeds, potentially reaching a substantial fraction of the speed of light. However, new research suggests that this approach comes with an unexpected complication. At extreme speeds, some of the very light driving the spacecraft forward could begin acting against it.

In a recent paper available on arXiv, Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology investigate how light interacts with a rapidly accelerating solar sail. Their findings reveal a surprising source of resistance that emerges as the spacecraft approaches 75% of the speed of light.

How Light Can Push a Spacecraft Through Space

Although light has no mass, it carries momentum and can transfer that momentum to objects it strikes. This creates a tiny pushing force known as radiation pressure. Under ordinary conditions, the effect is extremely weak, but in the vacuum of space, a large reflective sail can gradually build up speed as light continues to strike its surface.

For spacecraft traveling between stars, powerful lasers could provide a much more concentrated source of light than the Sun. By directing an intense beam at a sail, engineers hope to accelerate extremely small probes to speeds that conventional propulsion systems cannot approach.

The researchers examined three ways that photons, the individual packets of energy that make up light, transfer momentum to a sail. These interactions are incident light (that raw momentum of the photons hitting the sail), specular reflection (momentum imparted when photons bounce perfectly off the sail), and diffuse scattering (momentum from photons that are absorbed by the sail then reemitted in random directions).

According to the study, these three contributions affect the sail's motion with different levels of efficiency. Incident light provides the strongest contribution in the researchers' breakdown, followed by specular reflection and then diffuse scattering.

A Strange Problem Emerges Near the Speed of Light

The situation becomes considerably more complicated once a solar sail reaches relativistic speeds, meaning speeds high enough that the effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important.

As the sail accelerates away from its laser source, it experiences an increasingly strong Doppler effect. This is the same basic phenomenon that changes the apparent pitch of a passing ambulance siren, except that light experiences a change in frequency rather than sound.

For the accelerating sail, the incoming laser light becomes progressively redshifted, meaning its frequency decreases from the sail's perspective. As a result, the light transfers momentum less effectively, reducing the thrust generated by all three contributions examined in the study.

In other words, the faster the spacecraft travels, the less effective its laser propulsion becomes. Even with a powerful beam continuously striking the sail, gaining additional speed becomes increasingly difficult.

Various concepts for interstellar exploration have been proposed over the years, including Breakthrough Starshot, which envisioned using powerful lasers to accelerate tiny spacecraft toward nearby stars. The new findings highlight another challenge that such ambitious missions would need to consider.

At 75% of Light Speed, Light Starts Working Against the Sail

The researchers identified an especially unusual effect once the sail reaches approximately 75% of the speed of light.

At this point, a phenomenon known as relativistic light aberration changes how the scattered light is distributed. Relativistic aberration describes how the apparent directions in which light travels are altered by motion at speeds approaching the speed of light.

From the viewpoint of an observer at rest on Earth, the diffusely scattered light becomes increasingly concentrated in the spacecraft's forward direction. Because emitting light carries momentum, the sail experiences a corresponding recoil in the opposite direction.

This means that diffuse scattering (admittedly the weakest of the three forces) begins producing drag rather than helping propel the spacecraft forward.

The result is a striking paradox: some of the light intended to accelerate an interstellar spacecraft actually begins resisting its motion.

Importantly, this does not mean the spacecraft suddenly stops accelerating or that its entire propulsion system begins pushing backward. The laser still generates a positive overall force, allowing the sail to continue gaining speed. However, the additional resistance reduces the efficiency of the system, making further acceleration more challenging.

Advanced Materials Could Help Overcome the Challenge

The study focuses specifically on the forces produced by light and does not attempt to model every obstacle a spacecraft would encounter during an interstellar journey.

For example, the researchers do not include resistance from interstellar gas and dust, which could become important at extreme velocities. They also leave out the thermal challenges associated with directing extremely powerful lasers at a thin sail. If the material absorbs too much energy, intense heating could damage or even melt it.

Another important simplification is that the calculations treat the sail as an idealized mirror. Real spacecraft would need materials capable of reflecting laser light efficiently while remaining lightweight, durable, and stable under extreme conditions.

Engineers are already exploring advanced metamaterials and photonic crystals that could help address these demands. These specially engineered materials can be designed to interact with particular wavelengths of light in ways that ordinary reflective surfaces cannot.

Intriguingly, such materials might even turn some of the relativistic effects identified in the research into an advantage. By carefully controlling how light scatters from the sail, future designs could potentially generate forces that automatically correct its orientation and position, helping it remain aligned with the laser beam throughout acceleration.

Despite the promise of laser propulsion, humanity remains far from building and testing a complete solar sail system capable of reaching another star.

The physics becomes increasingly complicated over such enormous distances and at such extraordinary speeds. Additional effects, including the curvature of spacetime, would also need to be considered in a more complete description of an interstellar journey. These effects were simplified out of the new analysis.

Nevertheless, understanding how light behaves when it interacts with a spacecraft traveling at a significant fraction of light speed is an important part of making interstellar exploration possible.

If humanity eventually sends robotic probes to another star, success will depend on solving countless engineering and physics challenges. Knowing that light itself can become an unexpected source of resistance gives researchers one more piece of the puzzle, and potentially a better understanding of how to design spacecraft capable of making the journey.

#628. The Killers’ Dave Keuning Says He Survived a Major Stroke: ‘By Some Miracle I Am Fine’

The guitarist says doctors gave him a 40% chance of survival — and that the first thing he checked after surgery was whether he could still play.

The Killers guitarist Dave Keuning has revealed he suffered a major stroke two weeks ago and went straight into surgery.

Keuning, 50, shared the news in an Instagram post on Thursday (Nov. 26), writing that a blood clot had cut off the blood supply to the right side of his brain. “Two weeks ago, I had a major stroke, and thanks to my wife acting fast, I went straight to the hospital and into surgery,” he wrote. “The first hour after a stroke is critical when it comes to getting to the hospital.”

“By the time I arrived at the hospital, I was blind in one eye and had lost function on my left side,” Keuning continued, adding that even then he didn’t realize he was having a stroke. Doctors gave him a 40% chance of survival and told him to expect lasting disabilities, he said, “but by some miracle I am fine.” Related Olivia Rodrigo Shares Second Holiday Song 'Miss This Christmas' on Amazon Music Fuerza Regida Announces 'Pisteando Con La Regida Vol. 4' After Partial Legal Victory Against Rancho Humilde Goo Goo Dolls Fans Slam NBC Over Thanksgiving Halftime Show Snub: 'Badly Handled' Explore Brandon Flowers Keuning The Killers See latest videos, charts and news

“And yes I can play guitar just as good as before,” he wrote. “It was the first thing I checked when I woke up from surgery.”

“I feel extremely fortunate that I am alive and well, and that I can use my hands and feet and talk just like before,” he added. “I am thankful for my wife, my son, my daughter, and all of my bandmates, who I feel closer to than ever.”

A founding member of the Las Vegas band, Keuning stepped back from touring with the Killers in 2017 and has stayed off the road since, though he returned to the studio for 2021’s Pressure Machine. He has also released two solo albums under the name Keuning: Prismism (2019) and A Mild Case of Everything (2021).

The Killers earned their first No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 2017’s Wonderful Wonderful and have notched eight No. 1 albums on the Official U.K. Albums Chart, most recently with 2023’s Rebel Diamonds. Their 2004 debut, Hot Fuss, produced “Mr. Brightside,” which in 2021 became the first song to log 260 weeks on the U.K. singles chart.

Brandon Flowers released his third solo album, Thrasher, in August, and has said he expects the next Killers album to arrive in 2027.

#627. Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria

The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought

The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data."

#626. Where to Watch the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade for Free to See Queen Latifah, LL Cool J & Dolly Parton Tribute

The centennial event will take place Saturday, Nov. 28, at 8:30 a.m. ET on NBC and Telemundo, but you can watch across several streaming platforms with a free trial.

All products and services featured are independently chosen by editors. However, Billboard may receive a commission on orders placed through its retail links, and the retailer may receive certain auditable data for accounting purposes.

This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is marking a few milestones: Its 100th anniversary and the first time in history that it’s ever been postponed.

Originally scheduled for Thanksgiving Day (Nov. 26), the parade was postponed to Saturday (Nov. 28) due to disruptions from strong winds and potential flooding across New York. Safety concerns surrounding the giant balloons also put their participation in question. The parade is scheduled to air live at 8:30 a.m. ET on NBC and Telemundo and stream on Peacock, though viewers should keep an eye out for weather-related updates.

Parade officials say that 95% of the originally scheduled acts will perform on Saturday. However, the Macy’s Great American Marching Band and the University of Alabama’s Million Dollar Band will be unable to participate due to scheduling conflicts. The lineup will also feature surprise additions from LL Cool J and Gloria Gaynor.

This year’s celebration is going big with a record-breaking 100 inflatables, including new balloons featuring Bluey, Hello Kitty, Mickey Mouse and Underdog. Music fans are in for a treat, with RAYE opening the festivities, followed by scheduled performances from Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, JoJo, RIIZE, EJAE, Keke Palmer, Anthony Ramos and Jimmy Fallon & The Roots. The lineup also includes a special Dolly Parton tribute by Megan Hilty and a Broadway showcase. Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker return to host NBC’s coverage, bringing viewers along for all the parade-day excitement.

#625. Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029

"The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?

Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.

That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.

Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.

Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."

The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.

In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

#623. Tyla & PARTYNEXTDOOR, Dolly Parton & Freddie Jackson Tributes & More Highlights From 2026 Soul Train Awards

During its celebration of "love, peace and soul," BET also revealed establishment of the Chaka Khan Humanitarian Award.

The Tyla hit “Chanel” was crowned R&B/soul song of the year and PARTYNEXTDOOR was honored as Spotify’s RNB X international artist during the 2026 Soul Train Awards. The Friday (Nov. 27) broadcast on BET and CBS marked the ceremony’s return following a two-year hiatus.

Pre-taped Nov. 5 at Chicago’s Harris Theater, the revamped awards ceremony — hosted by Anthony Anderson — only featured the two aforementioned fan-voted categories. Those awards were presented by LisaRaye McCoy and Chance the Rapper, respectively. While Tyla and PARTYNEXTDOOR weren’t there to accept their awards, the theater’s in-house audience and broadcast viewers were treated to special award tributes to and performances by Classic Soul Award honoree Chaka Khan, New Soul honoree Elmiene and Soul Personified honoree Durand Bernarr. Also performing on the two-hour show were Lucky Daye, Muni Long, JayDon and Jai’Len Josey — the latter two of whom were the next-gen talents showcased during the BET Amplified segments.

Among the highlights rounding out the broadcast was the return of a Soul Train Awards tradition, the Soul Cypher. As host Anderson noted in his introduction, it was Grammy-winning artist Erykah Badu who called out the need for a cypher back in 2015. Representing R&B’s foundational roots and ongoing evolution, the talented cast tapped for the Spotify-presented “Badu’s Soul Cypher” included Rapsody, Dave Hollister, CeeLo Green and Avery Wilson alongside Badu.

Below are four additional highlights from BET’s 2026 Soul Train Awards.

Beyond the presented awards, the ceremony also paid tribute to the late Don Cornelius via vintage video clips and photos as well as comments made by the performers and presenters. It was Cornelius who created and hosted the original Soul Train dance show in Chicago in 1970. Expanding into national syndication a year later, Soul Train — which relocated to Los Angeles and ended in 2006 — became must-see TV every Saturday thanks to the diverse array of prominent Black and white acts who performed on the show encompassing R&B/soul, pop, funk, hip-hop and other genres. Not to mention the introduction of popular staples such as the Soul Train dance line and scramble board while providing weekly commentary on the latest fashion styles and other popular cultural trends. With the advent of the Soul Train Music Awards in 1987, the pioneering dance show further cemented its now 56-year legacy.

If anyone can jumpstart an audience and get them up on their feet, it’s Kirk Franklin. Following a video spotlighting Soul Train’s storied legacy, gospel icon opened the show with an energetic and dance-fueled performance of “This Time.” The song, which features a guest turn by rapper GloRilla, is one of the tracks from Franklin’s latest album, I Am What I Am. Stepping onstage to join Franklin was host Anderson. Sporting jeans and a denim vest over a close-fitting white T-shirt as was Franklin, the actor/comedian performed a customized rap to the audience’s surprise and delight: “Soul Train is back / Tell me can you feel this/ Kiss the ring of the godfather, Don Cornelius/ Celebrating R&B at its highest form/ Kick it off with some gospel/ Get the stage warm.” Anderson’s rap also included comedic verses that drew raucous audience laughter like asking Franklin, “But bro, how do you perform with this tight shirt/ My circulation’s bad/ You know, I got the sugars, dawg.”

During an interview ahead of the awards show, BET executive vp, specials, music programming & music strategy Connie Orlando told Billboard, “We’ve learned over the last couple of years that finding a bridge for the generations is important as is honoring [legacies].” Following that strategy, this year’s ceremony recognized three phases in R&B/soul’s continuing legacy: Classic Soul, New Soul and Soul Personified. While each of the respective honorees — Chaka Khan, Elmiene and Durand Bernarr — performed, their acceptance speeches were impactful.

While presenting Khan’s honor, Common revealed that BET has also established the Chaka Khan Humanitarian Award. To be annually at the Soul Train Awards beginning in 2027, the award will honor the humanitarian, community service and social justice contributions of musicians and cultural figures. The award stems from Khan’s longstanding humanitarian work through her 1999-founded Chaka Khan Foundation. Reflecting on her 50-year career, Khan — who closed the show with a performance including her classics “I’m Every Woman” and “Through the Fire” — commented, “I’m most honored … Soul music is more than something we sing. It’s our history, our joy and our pain. It’s our churches and our love for one another. To the young people coming up: stand strong, keep your voice and follow your heart … We’ve still got so much music to make and so much love to give … We’re not finished yet.”

Accompanying himself on piano, Elmiene sang “Honour” from his 2026 debut album, sounds for someone to resounding applause. “I want to dedicate my award and the next 15 awards of mine to my hero D’Angelo,” said the British-Sudanese singer-songwriter. “Singing his songs is the reason I’m here. He was the person who put me on my path to ever be a musician and to ever write any note or song … To stand here and be even a little bit close to my hero, I really want to thank all of you.”

Newly minted 2027 Grammy nominee (and 2026 first-time winner) Bernarr delivered a riveting performance of “My Life” from his latest album BERNARR before accepting his award from Muni Long. “There are people in this room whose voices reached me long before mine ever reached you,” said Bernarr. “Being honored among you means more than I can put into words … Don Cornelius understood the power of recognition. Soul Train brought Black brilliance into our homes and gave us permission to imagine ourselves inside of it. We’ve seen what happens when people recognize their power and move together. We turn hope into action, conviction into change and even red states blue. BET and Soul Train, thank you for giving my voice a place in this legacy.” Then hoisting his trophy in the air, Bernarr ended with Cornelius’ signature Soul Train sign-off: “Love, peace and soul!”

While some might have questioned Dolly Parton being saluted at the Soul Train Awards, Anderson spoke about the country legend’s commitment to the Black community. Citing Whitney Houston’s cover of the Parton-penned “I Will Always Love You,” Anderson noted that Parton put the proceeds from that Houston global smash “right back into our community.” Sharing a Parton comment dating back to 2020, Anderson said, “She stood with us. I quote [Parton who said] ‘Of course, Black Lives Matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No.’” Steel guitarist Robert Randolph (who played with Parton) then took the stage with artists Brittney Spencer and Mickey Guyton whose roof-raising rendition of the Parton classic “Jolene” sparked an audience singalong. As did El DeBarge’s salute to R&B king Freddie Jackson who, said Anderson, “made slow dancing an artform.” DeBarge delivered an stirring performance of “You Are My Lady,” one of the late singer’s 10 No. 1 R&B hits.

#622. After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an important milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

The telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years

For its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

By examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

The main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

One important measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Professor Bunce said: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is new!

"During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

The results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

The team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector shows no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry

BepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

One of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

The instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

The telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal important connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy

For Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Dr. Martindale said: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was launched.

"This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit."

The milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations."

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

The mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

#621. RAYE Sets the Mood at 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade With ‘Joy’

The British singer-songwriter performed alongside her sisters, Amma and Absolutely, in New York City on Nov. 28.

RAYE helped usher in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade with a performance of her song “Joy.”

Dressed in a dark brown ensemble, the 29-year-old British singer-songwriter performed the track alongside her sisters, Amma and Absolutely, from a Central Park tunnel in New York City on Saturday (Nov. 28).

The uplifting track appears on her 2026 album, This Music May Contain Hope, and was among the songs recognized in the 2027 Grammy Awards’ songwriter of the year, non-classical, nomination.

RAYE performed center stage with a sharply dressed band behind her, while large columns and a staircase served as the backdrop. It was unclear at press time whether the performance was live or prerecorded following changes to the parade’s schedule.

The 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was originally scheduled for Thursday (Nov. 26), in keeping with its annual tradition, but was postponed to Saturday due to severe weather.

The performance comes amid a standout year for RAYE, who topped the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods, the most of any artist.

Her second album, This Music May Contain Hope, debuted at No. 11 on the Billboard 200 and topped the U.K.’s Official Albums Chart in April, earning the singer her first No. 1 album in her home country.

The album has marked a milestone year for RAYE, who also graced the cover of Billboard’s Indie Power Players issue, took home the prestigious Mercury Prize and landed her feature film acting debut in the upcoming thriller Lineage.

Among RAYE’s 11 Grammy nominations are record and song of the year for her Billboard Hot 100 No. 11 hit “Where Is My Husband!” and album of the year and best pop vocal album for This Music May Contain Hope. She is also nominated for songwriter of the year, non-classical, as well as best pop duo/group performance, best music video and best arrangement, instruments and vocals for “Click Clack Symphony” featuring Hans Zimmer.

The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade aired on NBC, Peacock and Telemundo, traveling from Manhattan’s Upper West Side to Macy’s Herald Square flagship store. The milestone celebration featured performances from a lineup of stars, including Billboard chart-toppers Megan Moroney and Teddy Swims.
